text: The most common flow failure isn't a crash, it's a pill that silently resolves to nothing, a required input nobody mapped, a condition that quietly takes the wrong branch, an approval that never resolves, or an integration step that can't reach the far end. Five real categories, each with its own tell in the execution log.

A null pill usually means a referenced record or field no longer existed when that step ran, not a bug in the pill itself. An unmapped required input fails outright with a named error. A data type mismatch sends an If/Else down the wrong branch with no error at all. A stalled approval was routed to the wrong person or an empty group. A REST step fails from an expired credential alias or an unreachable external system.

Picture a flow that triggers on record creation, then three steps later references a related record. If that related record gets deleted in between, the pill simply resolves to null — no error thrown, just unpredictable downstream behavior depending on that value. An unmapped required input is more obvious: the action fails outright, and the execution log names the exact input that was never given a data pill.

A number field compared against a string value in an If/Else looks fine on the design canvas but evaluates differently than you'd expect. There's no error message here — only the wrong branch running. Inspecting both resolved values in the execution log is the only reliable way to catch it. A stalled approval looks similar from the outside: the run just sits there, except here the log shows a waiting status at the approval step with an empty or misdirected approver pill, not a comparison gone wrong.

A REST step calling an external system adds one more wrinkle: the log shows the failure directly on that step, and the message itself tells you which half broke — an authentication error points to an expired or invalid Connection & Credential Alias, while a timeout or an error response points to the external system being unreachable. Diagnosing any of these five follows the same method: open the run, find exactly where it stopped or paused, read the actual resolved values at that point, and match what you see to one of the categories, rather than guessing which one you're facing.
Next, a full worked scenario: a stuck onboarding flow, diagnosed step by step using exactly this method.
